deep.reconstruction:
This page studies the Teichmüller tower in modular dimension 1, meaning the sphere with 4 marked points (T_{0,4}) and the once-punctured torus (T_{1,1}). It links them through the combinatorics of a 4-element set and the tetrahedron/cube maps from the previous page.

(1) Pictures. A sphere has 4 marked points a, b, c, d on the equator. The equator is the reference circle: it separates {a,b} from {c,d}, so it is a pants decomposition of S_{0,4} (one essential curve).
- σ (left arrow) is an elementary move to another decomposition. The red meridian is the new curve. The resulting move, or the resulting picture, is labelled l.
- ρ (up arrow) gives pictures with two curves and a tetrahedron sketch.
- The down arrow gives the 'complete' picture with all three curves, again with a tetrahedron sketch.
- The faint pictures at the far left and right show degenerations: the sphere pinched into two spheres, and the curve pinched.
The boxed relations ρ^3 = σ^2 = 1, ρσ = l are the presentation PSL(2,Z) = Z/3 * Z/2. Here l is the infinite-order (parabolic, i.e. twist-type) product of the order-3 and order-2 generators. This is the presentation of T'_{04} ≅ PSL(2,Z) ≅ T_{1,1}/{±1}, read off the 'Lego' moves on S_{0,4}.

(2) Combinatorics of I = {a,b,c,d}. 𝔍 is the 3-element set of partitions of I into two pairs:
- Q_0 = (ad)(bc), Q_1 = (bd)(ac), Q_∞ = (cd)(ab).
The labels 0, 1, ∞ are the values of the cross-ratio at which the corresponding pair of points coalesces, i.e. the three cusps of M_{0,4} = P^1 − {0,1,∞}.

For Q ∈ 𝔍, D_Q is its set of two blocks. Then:
- I = ⊔_{d∈D_Q} d.
- A_Q = ∏ d (a 4-element set of transversals).
- C_Q = ∧ d is a 2-element set, presumably the 'orientation/sign' torsor.
- ω_Q = C_Q ∧ D_Q.
- He claims ω_I = ω_𝔍 ≅ C_Q ≅ 𝔍 − {Q}. This is a canonical identification of 2-element sets (orientations of I versus orientations of 𝔍) with the two other partitions.

The exact sequence 0 → V(𝔍) → 𝔊_I → 𝔊_𝔍 → 1 is the classical S_4 → S_3 with Klein four-group kernel. V(𝔍) is a 2-dimensional F_2-vector space whose nonzero vectors are the elements of 𝔍. This gives S_4 ≅ Aff(2, F_2) and S_3 ≅ SL(2, F_2) = GL(2, F_2).

The line '(oriented tetrahedron + diagonal) ↔ (square + codiagonal)', with ≅ ω_I × 𝔍 ≅ 𝔍 × ω_I, counts the relevant marked maps (the tetrahedral and cube/square cartographic structures of p.18) as torsors under ω_I × 𝔍. There are 6 of them.

(3) The diagram of extensions:
- Top row: T^!_{0,4} → T_{04} → 𝔊_4 ≅ Aff(2, Z/2) → 1. The pure mapping class group sits in the full one with quotient S_4.
- Middle row: 1 → π_{0,3} → T'_{04} → 𝔊_3 ≅ SL(2, Z/2) → 1. Here T'_{04} = T_{04}/V ≅ PSL(2,Z), and the pure group π_{0,3} = π_1(P^1 − 3 points) ≅ F_2 ≅ PΓ(2) ≅ T^!_{0,4}.
- Bottom row: 1 → π^{(2)}_{0,3} → T_{1,1} ≅ SL(2,Z) → 𝔊̃_3 → 1.

The square T_{04} → T'_{04}, 𝔊_4 → 𝔊_3 is marked 'cart' (cartesian): T_{04} = T'_{04} ×_{𝔊_3} 𝔊_4. The up-arrows come from the hyperelliptic double cover. An elliptic curve is a double cover of P^1 branched at 4 points (or 3 points plus one fixed point), giving SL(2,Z) → PSL(2,Z) with kernel ±1. The kernel π^{(2)}_{0,3} is required to map isomorphically onto π_{0,3}.

This forces 𝔊̃_3 to be a central Z/2-extension of S_3 of order 12 in which −1 survives: the binary dihedral group Dic_3. Indeed S ↦ x (order 4) and ST ↦ a (order 6) give a surjection SL(2,Z) → Dic_3 with torsion-free kernel of index 12, hence free of rank 2 (χ = 12·(−1/12) = −1). This kernel is Γ(2) ∩ ker(SL(2,Z) → Z/4), a level-4 congruence subgroup. So 𝔊̃_3 is a quotient of SL(2, Z/4Z), consistent with Grothendieck's 'Sl(2, Z/4Z)/−'.

Purpose: to set up the basic building block (modular dimension 1) of the Teichmüller tower / Lego game. That means identifying the generators and relations of T_{0,4} and T_{1,1} with the tetrahedral/cube combinatorial maps, and relating the genus-0 and genus-1 groups by explicit group extensions.
errors: '𝔊̃_3 ≃ Sl(2, Z/4Z)/−' cannot mean the quotient by ±1 if the kernel is to be isomorphic to π_{0,3}. SL(2, Z/4)/{±1} has order 24, and the corresponding kernel ±Γ(4) is not free of rank 2. For the vertical isomorphism π_{0,3} ≅ π^{(2)}_{0,3} to hold, 𝔊̃_3 must have order 12 (binary dihedral Dic_3, a quotient of SL(2, Z/4)). The notation '/−' is ambiguous rather than clearly wrong.

The definitions of C_Q = ∧ d and ω_Q = C_Q ∧ D_Q are too terse to verify. The asserted canonical bijections ω_I ≅ C_Q ≅ 𝔍 − {Q} are plausible as identifications of 2-element sets but not proved on the page.

ideas.what: Presentation of the modular group via moves on S_{0,4}: ρ^3 = σ^2 = 1, ρσ = l (twist)
ideas.modern_name: PSL(2,Z) ≅ Z/3 * Z/2; Lego/Moore–Seiberg-type relations in modular dimension 1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Klein, Fricke); as Lego relations: Grothendieck (Esquisse), Moore–Seiberg, Hatcher–Thurston, Bakalov–Kirillov
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), discussion of the Teichmüller tower in modular dimension 1

ideas.what: Three pair-partitions of {a,b,c,d} labelled 0, 1, ∞ as the cusps / pants decompositions of S_{0,4}
ideas.modern_name: Pants decompositions of S_{0,4} ↔ cusps of M_{0,4}; Farey/curve complex vertices
Klein four-group extension; exceptional isomorphism S_4 ≅ AGL(2,2)

ideas.what: Cartesian square T_{04} = T'_{04} ×_{S_3} S_4 and the comparison of T_{0,4}, PSL(2,Z), SL(2,Z) = T_{1,1} via the hyperelliptic cover
ideas.modern_name: Mod(S_{0,4}) ≅ PSL(2,Z) ⋉ (Z/2)^2; Birman–Hilden relation Mod(S_{1,1}) → Mod(S_{0,4})
ideas.where_published: Esquisse mentions T_{0,4} and T_{1,1} as the modular-dimension-1 pieces, without this diagram

ideas.what: Free normal subgroup π^{(2)}_{0,3} of SL(2,Z), isomorphic to π_{0,3}, with order-12 quotient (a central double cover of S_3, via SL(2, Z/4))
ideas.modern_name: Torsion-free level-4 congruence subgroup lifting PΓ(2); quotient binary dihedral Dic_3

ideas.what: Correspondence (oriented tetrahedron + diagonal) ↔ (square + codiagonal), as torsor under ω_I × 𝔍
ideas.modern_name: Dessins/cartographic structures on the sphere with 4 points (tetrahedral and cube maps)

missed.claim: An explicit worked diagram linking T_{0,4}, PSL(2,Z) and T_{1,1} through cartesian squares over S_4 → S_3. In it, the genus-0 pure group π_{0,3} lifts to a free normal subgroup of SL(2,Z) with a level-4 finite quotient (a double cover of S_3). This is a documentary detail of how Grothendieck set up the base of the Lego game; the mathematics itself is classical.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest for the genesis of the Teichmüller-tower / Grothendieck–Teichmüller program. It shows the genus-0 and genus-1 modular-dimension-1 pieces being glued by explicit finite-group data, as later formalized in GT-group work (Drinfeld, Ihara, Lochak–Schneps, Hatcher–Lochak–Schneps). No new theorem.

deep.surprise_reason: All content is classical: the PSL(2,Z) presentation, S_4 ≅ AGL(2,F_2), Mod(S_{0,4}) versus SL(2,Z), and congruence quotients. It is set in Grothendieck's own combinatorial framework (tetrahedral/cube maps, cusps 0, 1, ∞). This is a nice working record but contains nothing absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: Top-left: 'I = 𝔍_Q = ⊔_{d∈D_Q} d' – the subscript Q sits under a Gothic letter; read as I written as the disjoint union of the blocks of Q.

Bottom diagram: 'T^!_{0,4}' is the pure (rigidified) group, preceded by a hooked arrow. '𝔊_4 ≃ Aff(2, Z/2Z)' and '𝔊_3 ≃ Sl(2, Z/2Z)' are annotations under/next to 𝔊_4 and 𝔊_3. 'cart' marks the upper square as cartesian.
Bottom row: kernel written 'π_{0,3}^{(2)}' (superscript partly smudged); T_{1,1} annotated '≃ Sl(2,Z)'.
Middle: the bracketed '≅ ω_I × 𝔍 ≅ 𝔍 × ω_I' sits under '(carré + codiagonale)'; the faint pencil above reads roughly 'tétraèdre + ... (carré + ...'; 'orienté' is inserted above 'tétraèdre'.
The faint 'D(Q)' near the box is a pencil note with a sketched parallelogram, not part of the formulas.
